title: What child protection training is mandatory for early childhood services in NSW?
description: NSW early childhood child protection training: section 162A courses, national child safety training, regulation 84 understanding and Child Safe Standards.
shortAnswer: Early childhood education and care services in New South Wales face three layers of training duty as at November 2026. Nominated supervisors, persons in day-to-day charge and family day care co-ordinators must complete an approved child protection course under section 162A of the National Law. Everyone working or volunteering must complete national child safety training on Geccko. Regulation 84 requires staff to understand child protection law, and the NSW Child Safe Standards require ongoing training.
keyTakeaways: In NSW, section 162A child protection training for nominated supervisors, persons in day-to-day charge and family day care co-ordinators means CHCPRT025 or CHCPRT026 (or a previously approved course); in-house training is not sufficient.

Since February 27, 2026, national child safety training is mandatory for everyone working or volunteering in NQF services: foundation courses within 14 days or before working directly with children, and refreshers every 2 years.
From April 24, 2026, NSW changes to regulation 84 require staff to understand child protection law, including being able to explain their mandatory reporting obligations and how to make a report.

Approved early childhood services must also implement the 10 NSW Child Safe Standards under the Child Safe Scheme, regulated by the Office of the Children's Guardian; Standard 7 is about continual education and training.
Advanced child safety training (courses 3 to 5) is due by March 31, 2027 for people already in relevant roles before September 30, 2026.
regulator: NSW Early Learning Commission (regulatory authority under the Children (Education and Care Services) National Law), with the Office of the Children's Guardian for the Child Safe Scheme
appliesTo: Approved providers and persons with management or control of NQF services in NSW, including long day care, preschools, family day care and outside school hours care
Nominated supervisors, persons in day-to-day charge and family day care co-ordinators
Staff members who work directly with children, and those who do not
Regular volunteers and students on placement for an approved early childhood qualification

sections.heading: What training obligations apply to NSW early childhood services?

blocks.text: Three separate instruments create training duties, and meeting one does not discharge the others. The NSW Early Learning Commission's [child protection and child safety training page](https://education.nsw.gov.au/early-childhood-education/regulation-and-compliance/regulation-assessment-and-rating/child-safety/child-protection-training-requirements) states that the national child safety training "does not replace the existing child protection training requirements", and both sit alongside the ongoing awareness duty in regulation 84 of the Education and Care Services National Regulations.

items: **Child protection training (section 162A of the National Law):** an approved accredited course for specified leadership roles, set in NSW by the Education and Care Services Government Protocol: Child Protection Training 2026.
**National child safety training (section 162B):** foundation and advanced courses on the Australian Government's Geccko platform, by role.
**Understanding of child protection law (regulation 84):** a continuing duty on approved providers, strengthened in NSW from April 24, 2026.
**NSW Child Safe Standards:** organization wide expectations under the Child Safe Scheme in the Children's Guardian Act 2019, including continual education and training.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects NSW Early Learning Commission, ACECQA and Office of the Children's Guardian guidance as at November 2026. NSW is implementing more than 30 legislated reforms progressively, and advanced child safety course 5 only became available on September 30, 2026. Check the primary sources before relying on a date.

sections.heading: Which roles need an approved child protection course in NSW?

blocks.text: In NSW, nominated supervisors, persons in day-to-day charge and family day care co-ordinators must hold an approved child protection course under section 162A, as specified by the Government Protocol. The Commission lists the approved courses as **CHCPRT025** Identify and report children and young people at risk, and **CHCPRT026** Support the rights and safety of children and young people, and states plainly that "in-house training is not sufficient".

The NSW Department of Education's own Child Protection Awareness Training is approved for department staff only, because it is designed for department run preschools inside primary schools. Superseded units such as CHCPRT001, CHCPRT002 and the older CHCCHILD units remain acceptable if a person in one of the three roles already completed them.

Other people, including approved providers, educators, employees, contractors and volunteers, "can meet their child protection training requirements by completing the prescribed national child safety training required under Section 162B", according to the Commission. That is a NSW specific arrangement: ACECQA's [national training page](https://www.acecqa.gov.au/national-quality-framework/child-safety/child-safety-and-child-protection-training) notes that Victoria and Queensland apply different child protection training rules, and NSW providers with staff moving interstate should not assume the same evidence transfers.

Section 162A sets no expiry date for a course or certificate. The Commission states that it "does not require 'refresher training'", but it recommends child protection refresher training every 12 to 24 months, and whenever child protection law or reporting requirements change significantly, to evidence regulation 84 and Quality Area 2.

sections.heading: What does national child safety training require, and by when?

blocks.text: From February 27, 2026, everyone working or volunteering in an education and care service regulated under the National Quality Framework must complete national child safety training. ACECQA states the training must be completed in Geccko, the Australian Government Department of Education's learning platform, and that "no other training meets the new requirements". It is free, and each participant needs their own account. The [Guide to the NQF](https://www.acecqa.gov.au/national-quality-framework/guide-nqf/section-4-operational-requirements/quality-area-2-childrens-health-and-safety) adds that authorized officers may ask for completion certificates and may check training details recorded in the National Early Childhood Worker Register.

items: **Foundation:** before the person starts working directly with children or within 14 days of being employed, whichever occurs first.
**Advanced, existing role holders:** anyone in a relevant role with their current provider before September 30, 2026 must complete it by March 31, 2027.
**Advanced, new starters:** anyone starting in a relevant role after September 30, 2026 must complete it within 3 months of being employed, engaged or appointed.
**Refresher:** foundation and advanced training must be completed again every 2 years.
**Transition:** people employed before February 27, 2026, or between that date and August 14, 2026, had until August 27, 2026 to complete child protection and foundation child safety training.

blocks.text: ACECQA states it is an offense for the approved provider to fail to ensure people complete required training within the prescribed timeframes. In NSW, the Commission notes that training requirements for relevant persons in family day care, including co-ordinators and those in leadership or oversight roles, apply from September 30, 2026 under the Education and Care Services (Child Safety Training) Order 2026.

sections.heading: What does regulation 84 require staff to understand?

blocks.text: Regulation 84 requires approved providers to ensure that nominated supervisors, staff, volunteers and students working with children understand current child protection law and their obligations under it. The Commission's [child safety reforms page](https://education.nsw.gov.au/early-childhood-education/regulation-and-compliance/regulation-assessment-and-rating/child-safety/child-safety-reforms) explains that from April 24, 2026, NSW changes require staff to understand child protection law, "not just be aware of it".

To meet the NSW standard, staff must be able to clearly explain three things: their obligations as a mandatory reporter, the circumstances that would require them to make a report, and how to submit a report. Providers are expected to build this into recruitment and onboarding, reinforce it through staff discussion and professional development, and "keep appropriate records of these steps".

This is a demonstrable competence standard rather than an attendance standard. A completed course certificate shows that section 162A was met; it does not show that an educator recruited last month can explain when a report is required. Services that want to evidence regulation 84 need a short, recorded check of understanding, which is the difference explained in [completion tracking vs competency verification](/compare/completion-tracking-vs-competency-verification). Health sector reporting duties are covered separately in [mandatory reporting training in Australia](/regulations/mandatory-reporting-training-australia).

sections.heading: How do the NSW Child Safe Standards affect training?

blocks.text: Approved education and care services must implement the 10 Child Safe Standards under the NSW Child Safe Scheme. The Office of the Children's Guardian lists "approved education and care services" among the entities that [must apply the Standards](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/child-safe-scheme/implementing-child-safe-standards/who-child-safe-standards-apply) through their systems, policies and procedures, and its sector guidance confirms that this includes approved early childhood education and care services.

Standard 7 is the training standard. Its published wording on the [Office of the Children's Guardian site](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/child-safe-scheme/what-are-child-safe-standards) is: "Staff are equipped with the knowledge, skills and awareness to keep children safe through continual education and training". Its three elements require training on the nature and indicators of child maltreatment, "particularly organisational child abuse"; training on the organization's child safe practices and child protection; and support for relevant staff to develop practical skills in protecting children and responding to disclosures.

Standard 5 adds an induction expectation: all staff and volunteers receive an appropriate induction and are aware of their child safety responsibilities, including reporting obligations. The Commission notes that NQF changes from October 1, 2023 to regulations 84, 149 and 168 brought the national rules into closer alignment with the National Principles for Child Safe Organisations, which embed the Standards.

Enforcement sits with the Office of the Children's Guardian. Its [monitoring and enforcement page](https://ocg.nsw.gov.au/child-safe-scheme/implementing-child-safe-standards/monitoring-and-enforcement) says it may request a "child safe recruitment, induction and training policy", inspect premises, direct a Child Safe Self-Assessment, issue a compliance notice or accept an enforceable undertaking, and issue fines if either is not followed.

sections.heading: How should a NSW service map these duties to roles and evidence?

blocks.text: The cleanest approach is one register per person that records each separate instrument, because the deadlines and evidence differ. The mapping below is original and illustrative, built from the Commission, ACECQA and Office of the Children's Guardian guidance cited above; it supports a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) and does not replace the law.

blocks.text: Because these deadlines cycle at different intervals (2 years for Geccko courses, a recommended 12 to 24 months for regulation 84 refreshers, none for section 162A), set each as its own [refresh cycle](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles). Screening is a separate duty: verifying a Working with Children Check is covered in [working with children check requirements](/regulations/working-with-children-check-requirements), and from April 24, 2026 NSW regulation 151 also requires each educator's check number on the record of educators working directly with children.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry separates the instruments, so a section 162A course, Geccko completions, a regulation 84 understanding check and Child Safe Standard 7 each appear as their own requirement with their own role scope, interval and evidence. The regulation 84 points (mandatory reporter obligations, when to report, how to report) become explicit assessment points rather than a line in an induction checklist.

faqs.q: Does Geccko child safety training replace CHCPRT025 for nominated supervisors in NSW?
faqs.a: No. The NSW Early Learning Commission states that the national child safety training does not replace the existing child protection training requirements. Nominated supervisors, persons in day-to-day charge and family day care co-ordinators still need an approved course under section 162A, such as CHCPRT025 or CHCPRT026. Other staff can meet the child protection requirement through the national child safety training.

faqs.q: Do one-off volunteers or parents need child safety training?
faqs.a: No. ACECQA states that one-off volunteers, visitors and parents or carers attending with their child do not need the training. Volunteers in an unpaid role delivering education and care on a regular or semi-regular basis must complete the foundation training, and providers should use professional judgment and a risk management approach when deciding which category applies.

faqs.q: Is in-house child protection training acceptable in NSW?
faqs.a: Not for section 162A. The Commission's list of approved courses under the Government Protocol states that in-house training is not sufficient for nominated supervisors, persons in day-to-day charge and family day care co-ordinators. In-house sessions remain useful for demonstrating regulation 84 understanding and Quality Area 2 practice, alongside the approved course.

faqs.q: Do outside school hours care services in NSW have to follow the Child Safe Standards?
faqs.a: Yes. The Commission states that early childhood education and care services in NSW, including outside school hours care services, are required to implement the Child Safe Standards under the NSW Child Safe Scheme. OSHC services regulated under the National Quality Framework are also subject to the national child safety training requirement.
